questions.question:
Explain what is meant by:
  1. a population
  2. a census
  3. a sample.
hints: A national census is taken every 10 years in the United Kingdom.
steps:
Distinguish the group of interest from how much of it is observed.

  1. The population is the complete set of people or items about which information is required.

  2. A census collects information from every member of that population.

  3. A sample is a selected subset of the population whose observations are used to investigate the population.

questions.question:
Explain what is meant by:
  1. a sampling unit
  2. a sampling frame.
hints: Number plates form a sampling frame for all cars in the United Kingdom.
steps:
Separate one selectable member from the list used to select members.

  1. A sampling unit is an individual member or item of the population that may be selected.

  2. A sampling frame is the list of all the sampling units from which a sample is selected, often numbered.

questions.question:
1. State one advantage and two disadvantages of taking a census.
  2. State two advantages and one disadvantage of taking a sample.
hints: Researchers have to balance time, cost, convenience and reliability of results when choosing methods of data collection.
steps:
Compare coverage, cost and representativeness.

  1. A census includes the entire population, removing sampling variability. However, collecting every response can be expensive and time-consuming. It is also unsuitable for destructive tests. A census can still contain measurement or non-response errors.

  2. A sample is usually quicker and cheaper, and creates less data to process. Its disadvantage is that it may not represent the population accurately.

questions.question:
E A sports club with 713 members wants to investigate the types of exercise its members do outside of the club.
  1. Suggest, with a reason, whether it is sensible to use a census to collect the data. (2 marks)
  2. Suggest an alternative method that the sports club could use to collect the data and give one advantage of this method. (2 marks)
steps:
Apply the cost and coverage trade-off to 713 club members.

  1. A census would take time because all 713 members must be contacted and their replies processed, so sampling is reasonable. Alternatively, a census is defensible if the club can easily contact every member and wants complete coverage.

  2. Take a representative sample of members; fewer replies make collection and analysis quicker and cheaper.

questions.question:
E A supermarket manager wants to test the softness of loaves of bread in the store bakery by squashing them.
  1. Suggest a reason why the manager should not test all the loaves of bread. (1 mark)
The manager decides to take a sample of 4 loaves and finds that 2 of the loaves meet the required standard of softness. The manager concludes that only half of the loaves in the bakery meet the standard.
  1. Give a reason why the manager's conclusion might be unreliable. (1 mark)
  2. Suggest one way that the manager can improve the reliability of the conclusion. (1 mark)
steps:
The test damages the product and the sample is very small.

  1. Squashing all the loaves would damage all the stock, leaving none suitable to sell.

  2. Two successes out of four gives a sample proportion of 1/2, but four loaves may not represent the whole bakery; the population proportion need not be 1/2.

  3. Test a larger, randomly selected sample drawn across the relevant batches.

E/P A manufacturer of light bulbs is testing the lifetime of the bulbs. The manufacturer switches the bulbs on and records the number of hours each bulb is lit before it blows.
  1. Explain why the manufacturer should take a sample rather than a census. (1 mark)
The manufacturer tests a sample of three bulbs and obtains the following results:
762 hours 851 hours 801 hours
  1. The company claims that the lifetime of its bulbs is 800 hours.
    1. Use the sample data to comment on this claim.
    2. Suggest one way in which the manufacturer can improve its prediction about the lifetime of a bulb.

Testing to failure destroys the bulbs; use the data cautiously.

questions.question:
1. Explain what is meant by a simple random sample.
  2. Explain how you would take a simple random sample of size 20 from a population of 100.
hints: You can use your calculator to generate random numbers.
steps:
Random selection must avoid duplicate units.

  1. In a simple random sample of size n, every possible subset of n population members has the same chance of selection.

  2. Number the 100 units 1–100. Generate random integers uniformly in this range, rejecting repeats, until 20 distinct units have been selected.

questions.question:
1. Explain what is meant by a systematic sample.
  2. Explain how you would take a systematic sample of size 20 from a population of 100.
hints: Work out the proportion of the population that you are going to sample.
steps:
Use a random start followed by a fixed interval.

  1. Systematic sampling selects units at regular intervals from an ordered sampling frame, starting at a randomly chosen position.

  2. Choose a random integer r from 1–5, then select r, r+5, …, r+95. This gives exactly 20 units.

  2. Choose eight distinct males and twelve distinct females by random numbers from the respective lists.

questions.question:
1. Explain what is meant by quota sampling.
Researchers want to investigate people's attitudes to advertising in the cinema.
  1. Explain how they might select a quota sample of size 30.
hints: Make sure your answer refers to the context of the question.
steps:
Quotas fix group totals but selection within groups is non-random.

  1. Divide the target population into relevant groups and recruit available people until the required number in every group has been reached.

  2. For example, use known proportions of cinema-goers in age groups to set quotas totalling 30. Approach cinema-goers, assign them to their age group and continue until each quota is full.

  2. State one key difference between quota sampling and stratified sampling. (1 mark)

questions.question:
E/P Amara is investigating daily total rainfall in Leeming in 2015.
  1. Explain how she can take a systematic sample of size 20 from the data. (2 marks)
She finds that on several days, the reading is recorded as ‘tr’. She discards these readings and chooses additional readings for her sample.
  1. State the meaning of ‘tr’, and evaluate Amara's method. (2 marks)
  2. Suggest how Amara should deal with ‘tr’ readings in her investigation. (1 mark)
steps:
Keep genuine low-rainfall days in the sample.

  1. In the ordered list choose a random starting position from 1–9, then take that date and the next 19 dates nine positions apart. Stop after 20 observations. A fractional-interval systematic design using interval 9.2 is also possible.

  2. “tr” means a trace of rainfall, less than 0.05 mm. Discarding these valid low-rainfall observations and replacing them biases the sample towards wetter days.

  3. Retain the dates and treat trace values as 0 mm for the prescribed calculation, noting that this is a small-value approximation.

questions.question:
1. Explain what is meant by a sampling unit. (1 mark)

  2. Give two advantages of using a simple random sample. (2 marks)
steps:
A simple random sample contains distinct, equally likely units.

  1. A sampling unit is one individual item or member of the population.
